metadata.title: On weight initialization in deep neural networks

nodes.statement: It is well known that arbitrary initializations can slow down or even completely stall the convergence process.
conclusions: It is well known that arbitrary initializations can slow down or even completely stall the convergence process.

nodes.statement: The problem can be stated as follows: If the weights in a neural network are initialized using samples from a normal distribution, calN(0,v^2), how should v^2 be chosen to ensure that the variance of the outputs from the different layers are approximately the same?
conclusions: The problem can be stated as follows: If the weights in a neural network are initialized using samples from a normal distribution, calN(0,v^2), how should v^2 be chosen to ensure that the variance of the outputs from the different layers are approximately the same?

nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of v^2 = 1/N, where N is the number of nodes feeding into that layer.

nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues argue that the itXavier initialization does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of v^2 = 2/N (commonly referred to as the itHe initialization).

nodes.statement: Using the recursions in () and (), x_m(k) can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first m-1 layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the m^th layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the m^th layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, W_m(i,j) is independent of x_m(k) for all values of i, j and k. Furthermore, since W_m(i,j) is independent of x_m(k) and x_m(l), W_m(i,j) will also be independent of x_m(k)x_m(l) linebreak Taking expectations in () and using proposition 1, along with the fact that E(bfW_m(i,j)) = 0 yields r_m = E(y_m(i)) = sumlimits_j=1^j=N E(bfW_m(i,j))E(x_m(j)) = 0. enumin201 Therefore, u_m^2 = Var(y_m(i)) = Eleft(y_m(i)^2right) - left(E(y_m(i))right)^2 = Eleft(y_m(i)^2right). Using (), u_m^2 &= Eleft(sumlimits_j=1^j=NbfW_m(i,j)x_m(j)right)^2 \\ &= sumlimits_j=1^j=N Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)^2x_m(j)^2right) + 2sum Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)x_m(j)bfW_m(k,l)x_m(l)right). \\ enumin203 From proposition 1, bfW_m(i,j) and bfW_m(k,l) will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of x_m(j)x_m(l). Using these results, along with the fact that E(bfW_m(i,j)) = 0 gives Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)x_m(j)bfW_m(k,l)x_m(l)right) = E(bfW_m(i,j))E(bfW_m(k,l))E(x_m(j)x_m(l)) = 0. enumin2041 Plugging () into () gives u_m^2 &= sumlimits_j=1^j=N Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)^2x_m(j)^2right) \\ &= sumlimits_j=1^j=N Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)^2right)Eleft(x_m(j)^2right) \\ &= Nv^2(s_m^2 + mu_m^2) \\ enumin204 for all i.

nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in , the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution left(U[-1/sqrtN,1/sqrtN]right) having a variance of 1/3N. Therefore, from () and (), with g(0) = 0 and g'(0) = 1, we have mu_m = 0 and s_m+1^2 = frac13s_m^2 < s_m^2 enumseq1 respectively. From (), this implies that u_m+1^2<u_m^2 for all m (i.e., u_m^2 is a decreasing function of m). Furthermore from proposition 2, y_m(i) sim calN(0,u_m^2). Therefore, x_m+1(i) will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable. Using results from , x_m+1(i) = mboxtanh(y_m(i)) will have a probability density function (pdf) given by f(y) = frac11-y^2frac1sqrt2pi u_m^2mboxe^left(-fract_y^22u_m^2right) enumtanh1, where t_y = frac12 lnleft(frac1+y1-yright). Plots of this pdf for different values of u_m (provided in Figure ) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure and figure 4 of suggests that u_m^2 is a decreasing function of m, as is expected.

nodes.statement: To understand why this happens, I compute the central moments of x_m+1 in terms of the central moments of x_m when v^2 = 1/N. From () we have u_m^2 = s_m^2 + mu_m^2. enumr01 Plugging results from () into () yields the recursion mu_m+1^2 = frac12pi(s_m^2 + mu_m^2) approx 0.16(s_m^2 + mu_m^2). enumr02 Similarly, plugging results from () and () in () yields s_m+1^2 approx 0.34(s_m^2 + mu_m^2). enumrelu5 Simple manipulations of equations (~--~) gives mu_m^2 approx 0.16 times (0.51)^m-1 enumrelu603 and s_m^2 approx 0.34 times (0.51)^m-1. enumrelu602 for all m geq 1. These approximations are remarkably accurate, as is demonstrated by comparisons with the simulation experiments described in Figure .
